---
title: "The Transcript tab"
description: "Read everything said in your project as text in the inspector, and choose which track and language the words come from."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

The Transcript tab shows what's said in your project as text you can read and click. It's the whole timeline as words, in the order you'd hear them, through every trim, speed change and nest.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Transcript"
  keys="⌃⌘T"
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript, between Document and the Assistant"
  tools={['get_timeline_transcript', 'get_transcript']}
  needs="A speech model on this Mac, or an AssemblyAI transcript of the file. No key is needed to read."
/>

<Shot
  name="11c-transcript-tab.inspector"
  alt="The inspector's Transcript tab, with the Words from and Language pop-ups at the top and the timeline's words below them in paragraphs, each led by its timecode."
/>

## Open the Transcript

Choose **View ▸ Transcript** or press <kbd>⌃⌘T</kbd>. The inspector opens if it was hidden, the tab shows, and the text takes the keyboard, so the [transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/) work at once. It isn't a toggle: choosing it again leaves the tab showing.

You can also click **Transcript** in the inspector's tab strip. That shows the tab without giving the text the keyboard, until you click in it.

The first time you look, the tab may need to read your files. See [Where the transcript's words come from](/captions/transcript-words/).

## Every word you would hear

The tab lists every word you'd hear if the timeline played, in order. That takes in clips on every track, and clips inside nests where they play.

It leaves out what you wouldn't hear: muted tracks, clips [soloed out](/audio/mute-and-solo/), clips turned down to silence and clips with their audio switched off.

With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open (<kbd>⌘↓</kbd>), the tab shows only what's inside it.

## Paragraphs and timecodes

The words come in paragraphs, each with its timecode above it. A new paragraph starts when:

- the words move to another track
- the speaker changes, which only a transcript from AssemblyAI can tell
- there are 1.5 seconds or more between two clips' words on one track
- the speaker pauses for 1.5 seconds or more inside a clip

A change of speaker starts a paragraph, and the tab doesn't print a speaker's name.

Some words show faint, and a pause over a second can show as a grey length such as "[2.4 s]". Those are about cutting. See [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/) and [Shorten a pause](/captions/shorten-pauses/).

## The bar

A bar sits above the text and stays put while the text scrolls. It holds the two pop-ups, then short notes on what the tab is doing and anything it couldn't read.

**Words from** and **Language** belong to the window. They stay while it's open, whichever tab you look at, and they aren't saved with the project.

### Words from

**Words from** chooses whose words to show: **All tracks**, the default, or one track by name. With one track chosen, the tab shows only the words on it, and reads only the files with a clip on it. If that track goes away, the tab goes back to **All tracks**.

### Language

**Language** chooses the language files are read in on this Mac.

**Automatic** is your Mac's language, shown in brackets as a code such as `en-US`. If you have no speech model for it, Automatic uses the closest one you have. Below it is every language your Mac has a speech model for. The pop-up is disabled when there are none.

Choosing a language reads the files again in that language. The earlier reading is kept too, so switching back is immediate. A file with an AssemblyAI transcript keeps showing that transcript whichever you choose.

### Read and Stop

While a file is being read on this Mac, a note shows its progress, with **Stop** beside it:

> Reading “interview.mov” on this Mac… 40 % (1 of 2)

**Stop** leaves the rest of the files unread, and the note changes:

> Stopped. 2 files not read on this Mac.

**Read** carries on from there, and so does coming back to the tab after looking at another one. Editing the timeline or changing **Words from** or **Language** doesn't start it again.

A file you stop part-way isn't kept, so it's read from its start next time. Stop only withdraws the tab's own reading: if an agent is waiting for the same file's words at that moment, its reading goes on.

## Clips with no words

A clip that can't give any words is listed under the pop-ups with the reason, such as "clip 12 — its audio is switched off". A clip inside a nest reads "clip 12 in nest Intro — …".

| The note says | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| its audio is switched off | Turn the clip's audio on. |
| its media has no audio track | Nothing. The file has no sound to read. |
| its media file is missing | [Relink the file](/projects/relink-media/). |
| it plays in reverse, so its speech cannot be transcribed | Turn off [Reverse](/speed/reverse/) to read it. |

The first three clips are listed. "…and 4 more clips with no words." stands for the rest, and holding the pointer over it lists them.

## The same speech on two tracks

When two clips carry the same speech, such as a camera's sound and a separate microphone, a note names the pair:

> Clips 3 and 7 carry the same speech. Mute one, or switch its audio off, to read it once.

Both stay in the text until you do. The note appears for clips of different files that overlap for at least 5 seconds, when at least 60% of the words of the clip with fewer words in that overlap also appear in the other.

## Good to know

- Nothing you do in the tab's bar changes the project, and the words aren't part of your edit.
- The tab has no search.

## With an agent

Agents read the same words with `get_timeline_transcript`, which answers the same notes and clips with no words, and can be held to chosen tracks or a language. See [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/).

## Related

- [Where the transcript's words come from](/captions/transcript-words/)
- [Follow along and jump](/captions/follow-the-transcript/)
- [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/)
- [Transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/)

---
title: "Where the transcript's words come from"
description: "How the Transcript tab gets its words, from an AssemblyAI transcript or by reading on this Mac, and what it keeps so the next look is immediate."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The [Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/) needs no setting up. It uses a transcript you already have, or reads the file on this Mac the first time you look. Either way it sends nothing anywhere.

<AtAGlance
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript"
  tools={['get_timeline_transcript', 'get_transcript']}
  needs="A speech model on this Mac, for any file with no AssemblyAI transcript."
/>

## AssemblyAI first, otherwise this Mac

For each file, the tab takes the first of these it finds:

1. **An AssemblyAI transcript.** You have one if you've used [**File ▸ Generate Captions…** with AssemblyAI](/captions/assemblyai-transcription/) or [**Remove Filler Words**](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/) on the file. Using it needs no key.
2. **A reading on this Mac.** Otherwise the tab transcribes the file the first time you look, in your Mac's language unless you [choose another](/captions/transcript-tab/#language).

Reading on this Mac is quick: about 0.7 seconds a minute of speech on an M2 Max, so an hour takes well under a minute. Playback keeps running while it reads.

The tab never makes a network request, whichever source it uses.

## One file at a time, playhead first

Files are read one at a time, starting with the one under the playhead. Each file's words appear as soon as it's done, without waiting for the rest.

If you switch to another tab, the reading stops, and it picks up when you come back. To stop it yourself, use [**Stop**](/captions/transcript-tab/#read-and-stop).

## Kept per file and language

What this Mac heard is kept in the project, one reading for each file and language, so the next look is immediate.

Each file is read whole, once. Trimming a clip, adding another clip of the same file or changing its speed doesn't read it again.

A reading is used only while the file and the macOS version are the same. If either changes, or you choose another language, the file is read again.

These readings are only for the transcript. [Captions](/captions/generate-captions/) and [Remove Filler Words](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/) never use them.

## When no speech model is installed

If your Mac has no speech model, the tab says:

> This Mac has no speech model installed. Choose File ▸ Generate Captions…, pick a language and press Download.

Do that, then come back to the tab. A file with an AssemblyAI transcript shows its words in the meantime.

A file this Mac can't read is named in the same place, and the tab carries on with the others. It tries that file again when you next come back to the tab.

## Ramped clips and following edits

Words are placed through a clip's speed, including a [ramp](/speed/speed-ramps/), so a word's time matches what plays on the timeline.

Editing the timeline updates the text right away, and the words you were reading stay where they were. During a drag, the text updates when you let go.

## With an agent

When an agent reads a file on this Mac, the tab's **Stop** leaves that reading running. The Assistant's own **Stop** ends it, and nothing is saved from a stopped reading. See [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/).

## Related

- [The Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/)
- [Transcribe on this Mac](/captions/on-device-transcription/)
- [Transcribe with AssemblyAI](/captions/assemblyai-transcription/)
- [Transcripts for filler words](/cleanup/filler-transcripts/)

---
title: "Follow along and jump"
description: "Watch the spoken word light up as the video plays, and use the transcript to move around the timeline."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The [Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/) stays in step with the playhead, and works the other way too: click the text and the playhead goes there.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Transcript"
  keys="⌃⌘T"
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript"
  tools="set_playhead"
/>

## The word being spoken

While the video plays, the word being spoken is highlighted. It stays lit through the pause after it, until the next word starts. Before the first word, nothing is lit.

The highlight follows the playhead when you're paused too, so moving the playhead by hand lights the word there.

## The text scrolls with playback

During playback the text scrolls to keep the spoken word in view.

If you scroll the text yourself, it stays where you put it for three seconds before it follows again. With playback paused, the text doesn't scroll on its own.

## Click a word to jump

Click a word to move the playhead to it and select it. The playhead lands on a whole frame. If the video is playing, it keeps playing from there.

The selected word becomes the timeline's in/out range, so clicking a word replaces any range you've set. See [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/).

## Click a timecode to jump

Click a paragraph's timecode to move the playhead to the start of that paragraph. Unlike a click on a word, this doesn't change the selection.

## A selected clip scrolls to its words

Click a clip on the timeline or the canvas while the Transcript shows. The tab stays, and the clip's first word scrolls to the top. The playhead doesn't move.

For a nest clip, that's the first word inside the nest. A clip with no words in the tab scrolls nothing.

## Loop plays the selected words

Whatever you select in the text becomes the in/out range, so [Loop](/timeline/loop/) can play it. Use it to hear a cut before you make it.

<Steps>

1. Select the words: drag across them, or click the first and <kbd>⇧</kbd>-click the last.

2. Turn on **Loop**, the repeat button in the toolbar.

3. Press <kbd>Space</kbd>.

</Steps>

Change the selection and the next pass plays the new range. <kbd>Esc</kbd> clears the selection and the range with it, and Loop then goes round the whole timeline.

## Related

- [The Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/)
- [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/)
- [Transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/)
- [Loop playback](/timeline/loop/)

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

---
title: "Edit captions"
description: "Change a caption's words, case, look, position and timing, and see which edits keep a word caption's word-by-word timing."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A caption is an ordinary text clip, so you edit it the way you edit any text clip. The one thing to watch is on a word caption page, where each word is timed to the speech: most edits keep that timing, and a few drop it.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Clip tab ▸ Text sections', 'Double-click a page on the canvas', 'The timeline']}
  tools="set_text"
/>

## Edit captions in the Text sections

Select a caption and open the **Clip** tab. The **Text** sections are **Content**, **Font**, **Style**, **Outline**, **Backdrop**, **Box**, **Reveal** and **Presets**, and they work as they do for any [text clip](/text-and-shapes/text-clips/).

Select several captions to change them together. That's the quick way to set a font or a colour across a whole run. Take care with **Content**, though: what you type there replaces the text of every selected caption.

To move a caption on the screen, drag it on the canvas or use the **Transform** section. To change when it shows, use the timeline, as [below](#trimming-splitting-and-moving-a-page). The **Presets** buttons set position as well as look.

## Change the words on a page

Type in the **Content** box, or double-click the page on the canvas and [type there](/text-and-shapes/edit-text-on-canvas/). The same rule holds in both places:

| You change | What happens to the timing |
| --- | --- |
| The text, keeping the same number of words | Every word keeps its timing. Fixing a misheard word is safe. |
| The number of words | The page loses its timing and shows plainly, with no word-by-word effect. |

Words are counted by the spaces between them, so turning "gonna" into "going to" changes the count.

A page that has lost its timing says **Not timed — regenerate to time it again** in the **Content** section. To time it again, [generate the captions again](/captions/restyle-captions/). That makes new pages from the speech, so any other corrections on those pages go too.

## Case on a word page

The capitals on a word caption come from its style, through the **UPPERCASE** box in the **Style** section. Untick it to show a page as written.

Case is applied when the page is drawn, so the **Content** box always shows the words as written, however the page looks. Changing case never drops the word timing.

## Trimming, splitting and moving a page

Trim, split and drag a page on the timeline with the usual tools. All three are safe for word timing:

- **Trim** changes when the page is on screen. Each word stays on the speech it times, and the page's text doesn't change.
- **Split** gives you two clips that play as the one page did. Both keep the page's words, each word still on its speech.
- **Dragging** a page moves its words with it, so they stay in step with the page, not with the speech under it.

## Reveals do not apply to a timed page

The text reveals (**Typewriter**, **Word Fade** and **Line Rise**) don't work on a word caption page. Its rows in the **Reveal** section are greyed, and the section says **Word style wins; the reveal does not apply.**

That's true of any page with a word style, including one that has lost its timing.

## Change a page's word style

No inspector section sets a word style's highlight colour, pop scale or pill colour. To change them, [generate the captions again](/captions/restyle-captions/) with a different style, or ask an agent.

## Newly revealed speech stays uncaptioned

When a speed-up or a ramp makes a clip play further into its file, the new part gets no captions until you choose **File ▸ Generate Captions…** again. [Captions follow a speed change](/speed/captions-and-speed/) explains how the captions you already have move.

## Word timings for agents

An agent can do two things here that a person can't: rewrite a page's word timings, and change its word style, both with `set_text`. Frame Job won't take a set of timings that doesn't have exactly one timing for each word of the page. See [Tools: text, shapes and clip names](/mcp/tools-clip-properties/).

## Good to know

- With an [action](/motion/actions/) selected on a page, a **Content** edit goes to that action and the page keeps its timing. Where the action's text has a different number of words from the page, the page shows plainly.
- A split page is two text clips, so an [exported caption file](/captions/export-captions/) has two cues with the same words.
- Frame Job won't run [Retime Range](/speed/retime-range/) over a caption page with timed words. Move the range off the page first.

## Related

- [Captions are text clips](/captions/how-captions-work/)
- [Word caption styles](/captions/word-caption-styles/)
- [Restyle a caption track](/captions/restyle-captions/)
- [Re-lay captions for a canvas](/captions/re-lay-captions/)
- [Export captions](/captions/export-captions/)

---
title: "Export captions"
description: "Write a track of captions out as a SubRip or WebVTT file to ship beside your movie, without changing the project."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Export Captions writes one track of captions out as a separate subtitle file, for a platform or player that takes one. Burned-in captions need none of this: they're part of the picture in any [movie you export](/export/export-a-movie/).

<AtAGlance menu="File ▸ Export Captions…" tools="export_captions" />

## Export captions

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Export Captions…**. It has no keyboard shortcut, and it's greyed out until some track holds only text clips, with caption text on at least one of them.

2. In the save panel, choose the [**Track**](#track) and the [**Format**](#format-subrip-or-webvtt). The name starts as your project's name with `.srt` on the end.

3. Choose **Save**.

</Steps>

Exporting changes nothing in the project, so there's no undo step. If the file can't be written, an alert says why.

## Track

The **Track** pop-up lists the tracks you can write, front-most first, with the front-most chosen. Each row reads like "Captions — 12 cues (track 4)". The pop-up is greyed when there's only one to choose.

Nothing marks a track as a caption track, so any track made only of text clips is listed, a titles track included. A track with any other kind of clip on it isn't listed, and neither is one whose text clips are all empty.

With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open, the list shows that nest's tracks.

## Format: SubRip or WebVTT

The **Format** pop-up offers **SubRip (.srt)**, the default, and **WebVTT (.vtt)**. Choose whichever your player or platform asks for. Changing it changes the extension in the name field and keeps the name you've typed.

The words and times are the same in both. The files differ like this:

| | SubRip | WebVTT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First line of the file | The first cue | `WEBVTT` |
| A number above each cue | Yes | No |
| Timestamps | `00:00:04,133` | `00:00:04.133` |
| `&`, `<` and `>` in the text | Written as they are | Escaped |

Both use LF line endings and end with one newline.

## One cue per text clip

Each text clip on the track becomes one cue, at the time and with the words it has now. A caption you dragged exports where you dragged it. Styling plays no part, so restyling a caption doesn't change the file.

- A caption with no text is left out.
- Line endings become LF. Blank lines inside a caption are removed, and so are spaces at the ends of its lines.
- A word caption track is written one cue per page, with the page's words as written. The style's **UPPERCASE**, the word timings and the styling don't go in the file.

## Frame-exact round trips

Export a track and [import it again](/captions/import-captions/), and every cue goes back on the frame it came from, at every ordinary frame rate.

The file itself may not match the one you first imported, because import snaps times to the frame grid. At 30 fps, `00:00:04,120` comes back as `00:00:04,133`. A file only comes back byte for byte when its cue times are already on the grid and a frame lasts a whole number of milliseconds, as it does at 25 or 50 fps.

## With an agent

`export_captions` never guesses the track. With no track to write, or with more than one and none named, it writes nothing and lists the candidates. See [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/).

## Related

- [Captions are text clips](/captions/how-captions-work/)
- [Import captions](/captions/import-captions/)
- [Edit captions](/captions/edit-captions/)
- [Subtitles](/captions/subtitles/)

---
title: "The Transcript tab"
description: "Read everything said in your project as text in the inspector, and choose which track and language the words come from."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

The Transcript tab shows what's said in your project as text you can read and click. It's the whole timeline as words, in the order you'd hear them, through every trim, speed change and nest.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Transcript"
  keys="⌃⌘T"
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript, between Document and the Assistant"
  tools={['get_timeline_transcript', 'get_transcript']}
  needs="A speech model on this Mac, or an AssemblyAI transcript of the file. No key is needed to read."
/>

<Shot
  name="11c-transcript-tab.inspector"
  alt="The inspector's Transcript tab, with the Words from and Language pop-ups at the top and the timeline's words below them in paragraphs, each led by its timecode."
/>

## Open the Transcript

Choose **View ▸ Transcript** or press <kbd>⌃⌘T</kbd>. The inspector opens if it was hidden, the tab shows, and the text takes the keyboard, so the [transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/) work at once. It isn't a toggle: choosing it again leaves the tab showing.

You can also click **Transcript** in the inspector's tab strip. That shows the tab without giving the text the keyboard, until you click in it.

The first time you look, the tab may need to read your files. See [Where the transcript's words come from](/captions/transcript-words/).

## Every word you would hear

The tab lists every word you'd hear if the timeline played, in order. That takes in clips on every track, and clips inside nests where they play.

It leaves out what you wouldn't hear: muted tracks, clips [soloed out](/audio/mute-and-solo/), clips turned down to silence and clips with their audio switched off.

With a [nest](/editing/nests/) open (<kbd>⌘↓</kbd>), the tab shows only what's inside it.

## Paragraphs and timecodes

The words come in paragraphs, each with its timecode above it. A new paragraph starts when:

- the words move to another track
- the speaker changes, which only a transcript from AssemblyAI can tell
- there are 1.5 seconds or more between two clips' words on one track
- the speaker pauses for 1.5 seconds or more inside a clip

A change of speaker starts a paragraph, and the tab doesn't print a speaker's name.

Some words show faint, and a pause over a second can show as a grey length such as "[2.4 s]". Those are about cutting. See [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/) and [Shorten a pause](/captions/shorten-pauses/).

## The bar

A bar sits above the text and stays put while the text scrolls. It holds the two pop-ups, then short notes on what the tab is doing and anything it couldn't read.

**Words from** and **Language** belong to the window. They stay while it's open, whichever tab you look at, and they aren't saved with the project.

### Words from

**Words from** chooses whose words to show: **All tracks**, the default, or one track by name. With one track chosen, the tab shows only the words on it, and reads only the files with a clip on it. If that track goes away, the tab goes back to **All tracks**.

### Language

**Language** chooses the language files are read in on this Mac.

**Automatic** is your Mac's language, shown in brackets as a code such as `en-US`. If you have no speech model for it, Automatic uses the closest one you have. Below it is every language your Mac has a speech model for. The pop-up is disabled when there are none.

Choosing a language reads the files again in that language. The earlier reading is kept too, so switching back is immediate. A file with an AssemblyAI transcript keeps showing that transcript whichever you choose.

### Read and Stop

While a file is being read on this Mac, a note shows its progress, with **Stop** beside it:

> Reading “interview.mov” on this Mac… 40 % (1 of 2)

**Stop** leaves the rest of the files unread, and the note changes:

> Stopped. 2 files not read on this Mac.

**Read** carries on from there, and so does coming back to the tab after looking at another one. Editing the timeline or changing **Words from** or **Language** doesn't start it again.

A file you stop part-way isn't kept, so it's read from its start next time. Stop only withdraws the tab's own reading: if an agent is waiting for the same file's words at that moment, its reading goes on.

## Clips with no words

A clip that can't give any words is listed under the pop-ups with the reason, such as "clip 12 — its audio is switched off". A clip inside a nest reads "clip 12 in nest Intro — …".

| The note says | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| its audio is switched off | Turn the clip's audio on. |
| its media has no audio track | Nothing. The file has no sound to read. |
| its media file is missing | [Relink the file](/projects/relink-media/). |
| it plays in reverse, so its speech cannot be transcribed | Turn off [Reverse](/speed/reverse/) to read it. |

The first three clips are listed. "…and 4 more clips with no words." stands for the rest, and holding the pointer over it lists them.

## The same speech on two tracks

When two clips carry the same speech, such as a camera's sound and a separate microphone, a note names the pair:

> Clips 3 and 7 carry the same speech. Mute one, or switch its audio off, to read it once.

Both stay in the text until you do. The note appears for clips of different files that overlap for at least 5 seconds, when at least 60% of the words of the clip with fewer words in that overlap also appear in the other.

## Good to know

- Nothing you do in the tab's bar changes the project, and the words aren't part of your edit.
- The tab has no search.

## With an agent

Agents read the same words with `get_timeline_transcript`, which answers the same notes and clips with no words, and can be held to chosen tracks or a language. See [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/).

## Related

- [Where the transcript's words come from](/captions/transcript-words/)
- [Follow along and jump](/captions/follow-the-transcript/)
- [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/)
- [Transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/)

---
title: "Where the transcript's words come from"
description: "How the Transcript tab gets its words, from an AssemblyAI transcript or by reading on this Mac, and what it keeps so the next look is immediate."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The [Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/) needs no setting up. It uses a transcript you already have, or reads the file on this Mac the first time you look. Either way it sends nothing anywhere.

<AtAGlance
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript"
  tools={['get_timeline_transcript', 'get_transcript']}
  needs="A speech model on this Mac, for any file with no AssemblyAI transcript."
/>

## AssemblyAI first, otherwise this Mac

For each file, the tab takes the first of these it finds:

1. **An AssemblyAI transcript.** You have one if you've used [**File ▸ Generate Captions…** with AssemblyAI](/captions/assemblyai-transcription/) or [**Remove Filler Words**](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/) on the file. Using it needs no key.
2. **A reading on this Mac.** Otherwise the tab transcribes the file the first time you look, in your Mac's language unless you [choose another](/captions/transcript-tab/#language).

Reading on this Mac is quick: about 0.7 seconds a minute of speech on an M2 Max, so an hour takes well under a minute. Playback keeps running while it reads.

The tab never makes a network request, whichever source it uses.

## One file at a time, playhead first

Files are read one at a time, starting with the one under the playhead. Each file's words appear as soon as it's done, without waiting for the rest.

If you switch to another tab, the reading stops, and it picks up when you come back. To stop it yourself, use [**Stop**](/captions/transcript-tab/#read-and-stop).

## Kept per file and language

What this Mac heard is kept in the project, one reading for each file and language, so the next look is immediate.

Each file is read whole, once. Trimming a clip, adding another clip of the same file or changing its speed doesn't read it again.

A reading is used only while the file and the macOS version are the same. If either changes, or you choose another language, the file is read again.

These readings are only for the transcript. [Captions](/captions/generate-captions/) and [Remove Filler Words](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/) never use them.

## When no speech model is installed

If your Mac has no speech model, the tab says:

> This Mac has no speech model installed. Choose File ▸ Generate Captions…, pick a language and press Download.

Do that, then come back to the tab. A file with an AssemblyAI transcript shows its words in the meantime.

A file this Mac can't read is named in the same place, and the tab carries on with the others. It tries that file again when you next come back to the tab.

## Ramped clips and following edits

Words are placed through a clip's speed, including a [ramp](/speed/speed-ramps/), so a word's time matches what plays on the timeline.

Editing the timeline updates the text right away, and the words you were reading stay where they were. During a drag, the text updates when you let go.

## With an agent

When an agent reads a file on this Mac, the tab's **Stop** leaves that reading running. The Assistant's own **Stop** ends it, and nothing is saved from a stopped reading. See [Tools: captions and transcripts](/mcp/tools-captions/).

## Related

- [The Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/)
- [Transcribe on this Mac](/captions/on-device-transcription/)
- [Transcribe with AssemblyAI](/captions/assemblyai-transcription/)
- [Transcripts for filler words](/cleanup/filler-transcripts/)

---
title: "Follow along and jump"
description: "Watch the spoken word light up as the video plays, and use the transcript to move around the timeline."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The [Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/) stays in step with the playhead, and works the other way too: click the text and the playhead goes there.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Transcript"
  keys="⌃⌘T"
  where="Inspector ▸ Transcript"
  tools="set_playhead"
/>

## The word being spoken

While the video plays, the word being spoken is highlighted. It stays lit through the pause after it, until the next word starts. Before the first word, nothing is lit.

The highlight follows the playhead when you're paused too, so moving the playhead by hand lights the word there.

## The text scrolls with playback

During playback the text scrolls to keep the spoken word in view.

If you scroll the text yourself, it stays where you put it for three seconds before it follows again. With playback paused, the text doesn't scroll on its own.

## Click a word to jump

Click a word to move the playhead to it and select it. The playhead lands on a whole frame. If the video is playing, it keeps playing from there.

The selected word becomes the timeline's in/out range, so clicking a word replaces any range you've set. See [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/).

## Click a timecode to jump

Click a paragraph's timecode to move the playhead to the start of that paragraph. Unlike a click on a word, this doesn't change the selection.

## A selected clip scrolls to its words

Click a clip on the timeline or the canvas while the Transcript shows. The tab stays, and the clip's first word scrolls to the top. The playhead doesn't move.

For a nest clip, that's the first word inside the nest. A clip with no words in the tab scrolls nothing.

## Loop plays the selected words

Whatever you select in the text becomes the in/out range, so [Loop](/timeline/loop/) can play it. Use it to hear a cut before you make it.

<Steps>

1. Select the words: drag across them, or click the first and <kbd>⇧</kbd>-click the last.

2. Turn on **Loop**, the repeat button in the toolbar.

3. Press <kbd>Space</kbd>.

</Steps>

Change the selection and the next pass plays the new range. <kbd>Esc</kbd> clears the selection and the range with it, and Loop then goes round the whole timeline.

## Related

- [The Transcript tab](/captions/transcript-tab/)
- [Cut by deleting words](/captions/delete-words/)
- [Transcript keys](/captions/transcript-keys/)
- [Loop playback](/timeline/loop/)

<system-reminder>
Contents of /Users/kevingalligan/devel/framejob/.claude/worktrees/help-docs/docs/site/CLAUDE.md:

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>

All five pages pass check-pages.mjs and docs_site_proof.py --pages with 0 problems. Anchors are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kevingalligan-devel-framejob/9cfd7405-83ec-4caa-905f-7b97a20f2cc9/scratchpad/inventory/anchors/captions-4.json (33 entries, every non-empty anchor confirmed to exist on its page).

One anchor differs from src/data/features.json: transcript-tab maps to "" (top of page) because the page has no "The Transcript tab" heading. If features.json keeps the anchor the-transcript-tab, full proof check D3 will fail until it takes this mapping.

Where the code overrode the guide or the brief:
- The guide's "Find (⌘F) does not search the transcript yet" became "The tab has no search", because the app has no Find command or ⌘F binding.

- The Reveal note shows on any page with a word style, including one that has lost its timing, not only on timed pages. The page says so.
- A Content edit goes to the action only when an action is SELECTED on the page. Nothing depends on the playhead.
- The tab doesn't print speaker names; a speaker change only starts a paragraph.
- Clicking a word sets the in/out range, replacing any range already set. The page warns about this.
- The on-device speed figure (0.7 s a minute of speech on an M2 Max) comes from the get_timeline_transcript catalog text. It is a measurement, so code cannot confirm it.

Added beyond the brief, from the code: a section on word style colours, the Retime Range limit on timed pages, and the note that a split page exports as two cues.
